folders.name: Settings
folders.about: Settings holds starting values the whole program shares: limits, names, lists of options. Only set values here. Nothing is shown or asked.

folders.name: Tools
folders.about: Tools holds reusable actions. Each tool starts with "define" and does its work in the indented lines under it. Tools only run when Main program runs them.

folders.name: Main program
folders.about: Main program is what actually happens when you press Run, step by step from the top.

examples.title: Get a number from someone
examples.say: ask for a number "How old are you? " and store in age

examples.title: Keep going until something happens
examples.say:
repeat forever
    ask "Password? " and store in guess
    if guess is "open sesame"
        stop the loop

examples.title: Make a reusable tool
examples.say:
define double using n
    give back n times 2

examples.title: Write it naturally
examples.say:
please ask for a number "Age? " and store in age then show age
if age is at least 18 then show "Welcome"
note: "please", "just" and "then" are fine. Filler is left out, and "then" splits steps.

examples.title: Use a tool and keep its answer
examples.say: run double with 21 and store in answer

examples.title: Keep a list of things
examples.say:
create list basket with "apples", "bread"
add "milk" to basket
for each item in basket
    show "-" and item

A blueprint for objects. Indent its fields and tools under it.
Named values bundled together, all public. Fields go under it.
Inside a class. Also "has whole number count starting at 0".
Inside a class: runs when a new object is made. Use "set self.name to name".

sentences.say: define ‹area› giving back ‹a decimal›, without changing the object
sentences.tip: Inside a class: a tool that reads the fields and never changes them.

sentences.say: make a new ‹Class› with ‹inputs› and store in ‹name›
sentences.tip: Creates an object from a class. Also "make a ‹Class› called ‹name› with ‹inputs›".
Brings in a library.
Write C++ directly.
Runs once, when the board powers on.
Runs again and again, forever.

sentences.say: skip the rest of this round
sentences.tip: In "over and over": the board starts the next round from the top.
Also "an input", "an input with pull-up".
And "turn pin 13 off". "the built-in light" is LED_BUILTIN.
On or off by a value (HIGH or LOW).

sentences.say: turn pin ‹led› on if ‹lit›, otherwise off
set the brightness of pin ‹9› to ‹128›
sentences.tip: 0 to 255, on pins marked ~.

sentences.say: read pin ‹A0› and call it ‹level› (a whole number)
sentences.tip: A0 to A5 read 0 to 1023; other pins read on or off (digitalRead). "read analog pin SENSOR" for a named analog pin; "… and store it in level" changes a name made before.

sentences.say: scale ‹reading› from ‹0›–‹1023› to ‹0›–‹255› and store it in ‹level›
sentences.tip: Moves a value from one range to another. Also "… and call it level (a whole number)".

sentences.say: set ‹duration› to how long pin ‹echo› stays on
sentences.tip: In microseconds: for distance sensors.
Or "wait 2 seconds", "wait 500ms", "wait half a second".
Millionths of a second, for timing a sensor's pulse.

sentences.say: if at least ‹500› milliseconds have passed since ‹last›
sentences.tip: On time without stopping the board. Also "more than", "less than", "at most".
Put it in "when the board starts".
Shows in the serial monitor. "show a followed by b" shows them on one line.
What is shown next carries on the line. "end the line" ends it.
Text with a value in it. "{t as text}" right after the text joins as "Temp: " + String(t).
For a decimal. "show ‹n› in hexadecimal" (or binary) shows a whole number in another base.
Fixed text kept in flash memory, so it takes none of the board's small working memory.
A library's start-up, in "when the board starts". "start pixels" if it needs nothing.
Add ", then start a new line" to move down a line (println).
Where the next thing shown goes: column and row on a text screen.
Make the servo first: "make a Servo called arm".
